Get started with DStressR

Source: vignettes/DStressR.Rmd
DStressR.Rmd

DStressR models reporter-activity responses in high-throughput reporter and chemical-genomics screens. It constructs growth-adjusted responses, estimates reporter-perturbation effects, moderates uncertainty, and returns reproducible hit tables with diagnostic plots. Growth summaries can come from any upstream workflow, including simple AUC or endpoint summaries and, when available, growth-curve models.

The package site contains use-case articles for the main analysis settings:

  • E. coli promoter-compound screen with empty-vector calibration
  • PFIbox fluorescence promoter-activity screen
  • E. coli fluorescence stress screen
  • Kochanowski promoter-activity compendium with supplied variances
  • Salmonella empty-vector-control screen-specific workflow

This vignette uses the public E. coli reporter-compound screen of Binsfeld et al. (2025), distributed with DStressR as a compact AUC-level data object. The data originate from the PLOS Biology supplementary data and associated Zenodo archive (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3003260; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15600688).

Input files and table shape

DStressR expects a long measurement table with one row per measured reporter-perturbation-replicate observation. In a complete rectangular screen, the row count is approximately:

n_reporters x (n_compound_wells + n_control_wells) x n_replicates

The table may contain additional rows when the same screen is repeated across batches, library plates, measurement plates, or experimental days. The important point is that these technical covariates remain in the table so they can be modeled rather than accidentally averaged away.

The required biological and technical information is:

  • reporter or reporter construct
  • perturbation or library-well identifier
  • reference perturbation, for example DMSO or water controls
  • luminescence summary
  • growth summary
  • replicate and optional technical covariates such as batch or plate

Column names are not fixed. They are mapped explicitly in prepare_assay().

Load the public E. coli reporter-compound screen 

library(DStressR)

screen <- subset(
  binsfeld_reporter_auc,
  strain == "WT" & removed == "No"
)

head(screen)

The table contains one row per reporter, drug or water-reference well, replicate, and serial-dilution observation. The original drug labels are retained, including Water_1 and Water_2; dose_level increases with compound concentration.

names(screen)
#>  [1] "strain"              "reporter"            "replicate"          
#>  [4] "well"                "drug"                "compound"           
#>  [7] "concentration_index" "dose_level"          "concentration_ug_ml"
#> [10] "od_auc"              "lux_auc"             "od_auc_per_lux_auc" 
#> [13] "removed"

Prepare the assay

prepare_assay() converts luminescence and growth summaries into a growth-adjusted log2 response. By default, DStressR estimates reporter-specific growth exponents from reference-condition wells and shrinks them toward a global reference-well slope.

assay <- prepare_assay(
  screen,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "drug",
  control = c("Water_1", "Water_2"),
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_auc",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "dose_level",
  replicate = "replicate",
  growth_covariates = "replicate",
  numeric_covariates = "dose_level",
  background_reporter = "EVC",
  background_by = c("drug", "dose_level", "replicate")
)

attr(assay, "destress")$growth_exponent_fit

To reproduce a fixed-ratio response, set growth_exponent = 1, which gives the log2(luminescence / growth) scale after the same optional EVC calibration.

Fit the model workflow

fit_destress() creates the fitted model object while accounting for technical covariates and retains the selected inferential configuration. results() then constructs the contrast-level inferential table, and call_hits() adds directional calls at a chosen false-discovery-rate threshold. The result table reports both the reference-relative total effect and the reporter-specific effect after subtracting the perturbation-wide effect.

fit <- fit_destress(
  assay,
  technical = c("replicate", "dose_level"),
  testing = "moderated_t",
  adjustment = "by_reporter"
)

tab <- results(fit)

head(tab)

The key columns are:

  • total_effect: reference-relative response for the reporter-perturbation pair.
  • global_effect: average perturbation-wide response across reporters.
  • specific_effect: reporter-specific deviation from the perturbation-wide effect.
  • specific_pvalue and specific_padj: test and BH-adjusted p-value.

The direct fitting functions remain available for existing scripts, but fit_destress() is the recommended entry point for new model-based analyses.

Empty-vector calibration

The Binsfeld screen contains an Empty Vector Control (EVC), which is used above as a matched background reporter during response construction. DStressR uses Huber calibration by default; least-squares calibration and direct subtraction remain available through background_method. The following call prepares the same assay without EVC calibration for a direct comparison.

assay_without_evc <- prepare_assay(
  screen,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "drug",
  control = c("Water_1", "Water_2"),
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_auc",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "dose_level",
  replicate = "replicate",
  growth_covariates = "replicate",
  numeric_covariates = "dose_level"
)

Call hits 

hits <- call_hits(
  tab,
  fdr = 0.05,
  lfc = 0.5,
  effect = "specific_effect",
  padj = "specific_padj"
)

table(hits$hit)
#> 
#> Downregulated        Not DE   Upregulated 
#>            21           618            19

In real screens, the FDR cutoff should be paired with domain knowledge and diagnostics. For reference-rich designs, empirical replicate/permutation p-values can be used as an additional calibration check.

Visualize the screen

The standard volcano plot labels the strongest reporter-perturbation pairs.

plot_volcano(
  hits,
  effect = "specific_effect",
  padj = "specific_padj",
  fdr = 0.05,
  lfc = 0.5,
  top_n = 8,
  top_reporters = 6
)

A response heatmap gives a matrix-level view of the reporter-perturbation response surface.

plot_response_heatmap(
  hits,
  value = "specific_effect",
  top_n_perturbations = 30
)

For broader screens, clustered heatmaps help reveal perturbation and reporter groups with similar response profiles.

plot_response_clustered_heatmap(
  hits,
  value = "specific_effect",
  top_n_perturbations = 30,
  title = "Clustered DStressR response map"
)
